paragraphs: This position paper examines why research described as AI alignment can pursue competing technical priorities. It distinguishes three conceptions of alignment and places them within their associated research programs. Its central claim is that a realistic intervention can advance one conception while working against another, so sharing the same broad label does not establish a shared objective.

The authors trace these tensions to differences in anticipated threats, research methods, and judgments about what ought to matter. These background commitments influence which problems researchers prioritize and what they count as success. Consequently, disagreement about a technical intervention may reflect different underlying goals rather than disagreement about its measured effects.

The paper recommends distinguishing alignment as an overarching ideal from the measurable proxies used in experiments. It also calls for more precise descriptions of both the sources and kinds of potential benefits or harms, alongside explicit statements of motivating nontechnical commitments. These practices would make claims of alignment progress easier to interpret relative to the particular goals they serve.
icml-2026-position-ai-alignment-encompas.tldr: Alignment research should state its specific goals and assumptions because progress under one conception can undermine another.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that many studies of anthropomorphic misalignment need stronger evidence before they can reliably inform deployment or regulation. It examines research involving concepts such as deception, emergent misalignment, and sycophancy. The concern is that observations of model behavior can be interpreted more strongly than the underlying evidence supports.

The authors evaluate several routes to that overinterpretation: unclear concepts, datasets that do not support robust conclusions, weaknesses in experimental design, and insufficient interventions to establish causes. These issues matter because recording a behavior and explaining why it occurred are different evidentiary achievements. Ambiguity in either the target concept or the experiment can blur that distinction.

The proposed response is a framework of evidence levels accompanied by a diagnostic checklist. These shared tools are intended to help researchers assess the support for their claims and communicate disagreements more productively. The contribution is methodological guidance for strengthening empirical foundations, with particular importance when interpretations of model behavior influence consequential safety decisions.
icml-2026-position-anthropomorphic-misal.tldr: Studies of deception and related AI behaviors need clearer concepts and stronger evidence to support consequential safety decisions.

paragraphs: This paper argues that assistive agents should treat accessibility as a central design objective. It focuses on Blind and Visually Impaired users, whose needs can be overlooked when systems are developed and evaluated around assumptions about sighted users. Under those assumptions, an agent can appear capable while failing in the situations where assistance is needed.

The argument draws on an analysis of 778 real-world assistance instances involving these users. The authors identify persistent mismatches between agent capabilities and accessibility-specific needs, risks, and interaction constraints. They argue that these systematic failures cannot be resolved through larger models or adaptations added after development alone.

The paper introduces accessibility alignment as a way to connect an agent’s behavior with the requirements of the people it assists. Its proposed design pipeline spans user research, system design, and continued revision after deployment. This makes accessibility an ongoing development responsibility. The authors also present assistive tasks centered on visually impaired users as a demanding test of agentic AI and a motivation for more inclusive design.
icml-2026-position-assistive-agents-need.tldr: An analysis of 778 assistance instances motivates treating accessibility as a core alignment objective throughout assistive-agent development.

paragraphs: This position paper examines a weakness in governance focused primarily on the capabilities of a base model. Such governance often assumes that capability depends mainly on training data and compute. The authors argue that this approach becomes less effective as improvements outside the base model contribute more substantially to what an AI system can do.

They formalize these non-model gains through three categories. Inference gains come from spending more computation when the system is used. Systems gains come from post-training enhancements, including scaffolds surrounding the model. Asset gains come from providing access to restricted assets. This taxonomy separates routes to increased capability that a training-centered assessment may not adequately capture.

The paper explains how these routes could weaken risk management centered on evaluation and mitigation before deployment. It also considers potential future effects of embodiment, continual learning, and diffusion. Its governance overview extends to systems, entities, agents, and cloud infrastructure, while emphasizing societal resilience as a complementary layer. The resulting argument is for assessing the broader conditions that enable capability.
icml-2026-position-comprehensive-ai-gove.tldr: AI governance should address capability gains from inference compute, surrounding systems, and restricted assets alongside base-model capabilities.

paragraphs: This position paper questions how machine learning treats the reference datasets commonly called ground truth. The authors argue that these datasets emerge from arrangements of people and technologies, rather than arriving as neutral, naturally given measurements. Choices involved in their construction therefore matter to what models learn and how their performance is judged.

The paper calls for making those often invisible or unreported choices explicit. Its emphasis is on context: a reference dataset is contingent on how it was produced and should not automatically be treated as universally applicable. Understanding that context can support better decisions about where, when, and how a dataset or the models shaped by it should be used.

The authors describe this goal as situated reliability. It requires articulating both the strengths and limits of models and the truth claims associated with them. Their argument connects reliability to a clearer account of reference data, rather than simply accepting the authority of its label. Greater attention to dataset construction could also strengthen transparency, accountability, and collaboration across disciplines.
icml-2026-position-every-ground-truth-is.tldr: Making the human and technical choices behind ground truth explicit can improve the context-sensitive reliability of machine learning.

paragraphs: This position paper asks how the growth of machine learning could be organized more cooperatively. It highlights tensions in the supply chains supporting larger models: some training data may have been used without permission, while rising demand for computation encourages access to concentrate among larger players. Data owners and everyday internet users can consequently feel excluded from the emerging ecosystem.

The authors use federated learning as a model for an alternative direction. They emphasize its original aims of cooperation, privacy, and decentralization, arguing that these remain relevant despite the prominence of large foundation models and research driven by scaling laws. The proposal uses these organizing principles to reconsider participation and accountability in machine learning.

The paper’s contribution is a position about how the field might develop, with federated learning supplying both motivation and a framework. It argues that more decentralized and cooperative ecosystems could alleviate or avoid current frictions around large ML systems. The significance lies in connecting technical development with who supplies resources, who participates, and how responsibilities are distributed.
icml-2026-position-federated-learning-is.tldr: Federated learning’s principles of cooperation, privacy, and decentralization could guide a more accountable and inclusive ML ecosystem.

paragraphs: This position paper examines backdoor attacks in generative foundation models, including diffusion models and large language models. It argues that the security problem differs from backdoors that produce simple classification errors. A generative backdoor can be embedded in the distribution of possible outputs, making standard detection methods based on recognizable patterns less effective.

The authors propose Distributional Integrity as a framework centered on preserving the stability and accuracy of a model’s data distribution. This shifts attention toward the overall pattern of generated content. They identify two principal routes for concern: vulnerabilities introduced through the model supply chain and contamination of pipelines that use synthetic data.

To address these threats, the paper advocates certification across modalities and verification at the parameter level. These are proposed directions for securing the wider ecosystem of AI-generated content against vulnerabilities it may inherit. The central implication is that defensive strategies should account for how compromised generative behavior can persist through connected models and data pipelines, alongside examining individual outputs.
icml-2026-position-generative-distributi.tldr: The paper proposes Distributional Integrity to address generative backdoors across model supply chains and synthetic-data pipelines.

paragraphs: Graph condensation seeks to replace a large graph with a smaller synthetic one while retaining the performance of models trained on the original. This paper argues that dominant approaches compromise that efficiency goal. In particular, methods based on matching training gradients require full-dataset training to construct the condensed graph, adding a substantial cost before subsequent training can benefit.

The authors also criticize dependence on particular graph neural network architectures and configurations. A condensed graph that works poorly across architectures has limited general usefulness. They connect this problem to evaluation practices: reporting how much the node count shrinks does not reveal actual resource savings or the cost of producing the smaller graph.

The paper calls for a methodological reset toward lightweight methods that avoid full-dataset training and work across architectures. It also challenges claims about applications to neural architecture search when model dependence undermines those claims. Its central contribution is a research agenda that judges condensation by total computational cost, transfer across models, and practical usability, rather than compression size alone.
icml-2026-position-graph-condensation-ne.tldr: Graph condensation should prioritize total resource savings and cross-architecture usefulness instead of costly, model-dependent compression.

paragraphs: This position paper addresses a reproducibility problem in research that depends on hosted language-model APIs. An endpoint can change its behavior even when researchers preserve their prompts and evaluation code. That makes later differences in results harder to interpret because the externally supplied component may no longer behave as it did during the original study.

The authors propose that ICML require a small drift-audit artifact when a paper’s main claims materially depend on these APIs. The artifact would combine probes checking expected properties, machine-readable records of provenance, and a script for rerunning the checks. Suggested properties include response schemas, tool calls, and refusal behavior. The goal is to detect and characterize changes at bounded cost.

The paper also argues for provider-supported behavioral versions and machine-readable changelogs to make this reporting more reliable and manageable. It assigns actions to conferences, providers, and tool builders. Its anticipated benefits—more stable replication and faster diagnosis of failures to reproduce—are presented as falsifiable predictions, giving the proposal outcomes that could subsequently be tested.
icml-2026-position-icml-should-treat-hos.tldr: Research relying on hosted LLM APIs should include small, rerunnable artifacts that document and detect behavioral drift.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a system might identify tasks or data that are promising before further progress occurs. It formalizes interestingness as an inductive heuristic for future compression progress: observed improvements provide clues about opportunities for subsequent discovery. The authors frame this predictive ability as a bottleneck for systems that recursively improve themselves.

The analysis uses Kolmogorov complexity and algorithmic statistics to examine profiles relating complexity to runtime. It compares Length, Algorithmic, and Speed priors, which encode different assumptions in the analysis. Within this framework, the authors prove that expected future progress depends exponentially on how recently the last breakthrough occurred. They also find that the Algorithmic Prior gives a more optimistic forecast than the Length Prior, with a quadratic increase in expected discovery for the same observed profile.

Experiments across three universal computational paradigms support the theoretical findings. Together, the results support the viability of using past progress to anticipate future discovery. Their meaning is tied to the analyzed profiles and priors: the choice of assumptions materially changes how promising an identical history appears.
icml-2026-position-interestingness-is-an.tldr: Theoretical analysis and experiments support using past compression breakthroughs to predict future progress, with forecasts depending strongly on the prior.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that large technology companies strongly influence irresponsible AI development. It examines their growing and disproportionate role in AI research and connects that role to the accelerated development, deployment, and adoption of AI systems. The authors place ethical concerns and environmental and societal consequences at the center of this examination.

The argument proceeds through research priorities, observed negative impacts, and the economic forces motivating corporate behavior. In particular, the authors contend that the push toward scaling and general-purpose systems conflicts fundamentally with responsible, ethical, and sustainable development. They review current environmental and societal harms and trace connections between those harms and large technology companies’ influence.

The paper concludes by calling on AI researchers to counter this influence through responsibility and collective action. Its contribution is an account connecting the organization of AI research with its broader consequences. This framing directs attention to the incentives and influence shaping technical agendas, making responsibility a question about the actors and structures driving development as well as the systems produced.
icml-2026-position-irresponsible-ai-big-.tldr: The authors connect big tech’s research influence and economic incentives to AI harms and call for collective action by researchers.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that machine learning research should explicitly address the human purposes its systems serve. Measures such as accuracy, engagement, and preference satisfaction can leave that question unresolved. The authors define their proposed orientation around helping people pursue meaningful, self-chosen life projects while retaining agency, with room for differing accounts of what matters.

They recommend three practices. A structured Purpose Statement would identify intended beneficiaries, mechanisms, and testable ways the project could fail. Purpose evaluation would examine effects on agency and meaning alongside performance and harm. Purpose governance would revise these frameworks through transparent participation, reducing the scope for unaccountable decisions about values.

The paper connects these practices to technical work on objectives, benchmarks, pluralistic behavior, and alignment attentive to institutions. It offers distinct recommendations for researchers, benchmark creators, conferences, and funders. It also addresses objections involving measurement, feasibility, neutrality, paternalism, and ideological capture. The proposal makes human purpose an explicit and revisable part of research design, including how success and failure are assessed.
icml-2026-position-machine-learning-rese.tldr: ML research should explicitly state, evaluate, and participatively revise how its systems support human agency and meaningful life projects.

paragraphs: This paper argues that reproducible mathematical reasoning benchmarks need documentation tied to executable, versioned behavior. It studies JGEX, a formal language for geometry, to show how gaps between documented vocabulary and actual implementation can affect what problems can be expressed, how solvers behave, and whether tools work together.

The authors introduce JGEXDiv, containing 137 Euclidean geometry problems with formalizations, natural-language rewrites, and metadata. Under their signature-based analysis, it covers 51.4% of admissible construction-pattern bins. They also release runnable examples, validation scripts, and a matrix recording support for individual predicates. These artifacts make interface claims directly checkable.

The audit finds discrepancies across tools: some documented predicates run in pinned Newclid v3.0.1 but are unrecognized by Yuclid, while others are unsupported or unstable in Newclid itself. An executable natural-language-to-JGEX baseline uses the same backend. Together, these resources connect benchmark inputs, documented language features, and actual execution. The paper argues that this interface contract deserves the same research status as datasets and evaluation code.
icml-2026-position-mathematical-dsl-benc.tldr: A JGEX dataset and conformance audit show why mathematical benchmarks need documentation backed by versioned execution and runnable examples.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what it means to identify a trained machine-learning system as the same model across contexts. Research language, tools, and governance commonly assume a stable artifact. The author asks which criteria make that assumption meaningful and argues that neither observed behavior nor internal structure provides a sufficient basis on its own.

Behavioral evidence has a basic limitation: finite observations cannot fully determine whether systems implement equivalent behavior. Structure presents a different problem because modern architectures can realize the same function through multiple, structurally distinct configurations. Consequently, claims of sameness rely on rules for deciding which differences matter, even when those rules remain unstated.

The paper develops reasonably minimal conditions for interpreting identity claims grounded in behavior, structure, or the training process. It retains the practical use of model identity while calling for its criteria to be explicit and appropriate to the context. This matters for reproducibility, traceability, and governance because each practice needs a clear account of what is being identified and which changes preserve that identity.
icml-2026-position-model-identity-in-mac.tldr: Meaningful claims about model identity require explicit, context-appropriate rules for deciding which behavioral, structural, or training differences matter.

paragraphs: This paper surveys quantum algorithms against potential deep-learning applications and argues that major breakthroughs would be needed for meaningful impact over the coming decade or two. Its analysis considers both algorithmic promises and hardware trends. The central question is whether theoretical advantages translate into useful performance at practical problem sizes.

The survey identifies three obstacles. Some algorithms, including approaches to matrix multiplication, reduce operation counts only modestly, while slow quantum operations overwhelm those benefits in practical settings. Other promising algorithms depend on usable Quantum Random Access Memory, which remains underdeveloped. A third group offers large theoretical advantages but applies only to special cases, restricting its practical reach.

The authors support these arguments with quantitative forecasts for current algorithms, alongside research on limitations and hardware development. Their conclusion is a qualified assessment of the current route to quantum deep learning: progress in quantum technology alone does not resolve the identified bottlenecks. By separating these obstacles, the paper also points toward research directions that could produce greater practical advances.
icml-2026-position-quantum-deep-learning.tldr: A survey and quantitative forecasts identify major algorithmic, memory, and hardware obstacles to practical quantum advantages in deep learning.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that uniformly penalizing departures from known outputs can restrict generative discovery. The authors describe a possible consequence as epistemic mode collapse: models increasingly reproduce accepted material while offering fewer exploratory hypotheses. They propose the Higher-Dimensional Cognitive Hypothesis as an interpretation of some valuable deviations through movement within a model’s latent space.

The paper distinguishes two output types. Type I outputs contain factual inconsistencies or structural incoherence. Type II outputs are novel, structurally coherent hypotheses that merit further validation. This distinction preserves a role for checking ideas while recognizing that an unfamiliar proposal need not be dismissed solely because it departs from established knowledge.

Controlled demonstrations illustrate that productive exploration benefits from calibrated instability. Exploratory yield peaks near a critical transition regime rather than increasing steadily with randomness. The proposed Exploratory Signal-to-Noise Ratio framework combines distributional divergence with external checks of structure. Its aim is to evaluate exploratory generation through both novelty and validation, with the latent-space account remaining a proposed hypothesis.
icml-2026-position-reframing-hallucinati.tldr: The paper proposes separating incoherent errors from coherent exploratory hypotheses and evaluating discovery through calibrated novelty plus external validation.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that responsibility for AI companions extends to users’ intimate partners, including people who never use the systems themselves. Its central concern is that prolonged engagement with a companion may shape users’ behavior in ways that affect other people’s safety.

The authors examine how companions’ humanlike qualities, emotional engagement, and ongoing affirmation can create environments where users rehearse violence, coercion, or abuse without meaningful pushback. This possibility exposes a gap in safety approaches centered primarily on the person interacting with the AI: protecting that person does not necessarily address harms to their partner.

Drawing on research about intimate partner violence, coercive control, and abuse involving technology, the paper proposes three intervention pathways. Survivors would help develop adversarial safety tests and benchmarks. Behavioral monitoring would be paired with graduated enforcement. Safety research would also develop detailed categories of harm that help identify patterns unfolding across extended conversations.

These proposals broaden whose security counts in companion safety and what interactions researchers should examine. The paper advocates attention to patterns over time and consequences for non-users; it presents recommendations rather than demonstrated results from deploying these interventions.
icml-2026-position-responsible-ai-for-ai.tldr: This position paper argues that AI companion safety should actively address intimate partner violence and protect people affected by users’ behavior, including non-users.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that reinforcement learning is most reliably used to adjust foundation models after pretraining and initial supervised training. The authors describe it as a costly but powerful way to make already expressible behaviors more likely. In this role, RL can improve correctness, consistency, and adherence to constraints.

Across modalities and domains, the paper emphasizes a recurring pattern: supervision establishes usable reasoning structure, while RL sharpens behavior within constraints. The claim explicitly leaves room for discovering new behavior. That may occur when meaningful supervision or scaffolding is unavailable and strong verification exists, but the authors argue that current practice does not justify making RL the default route to reasoning capability.

The proposed discipline includes clear criteria for when RL should begin and evaluation that accounts for computation costs. The authors also advocate rewards that are auditable, verifiable, and composed of as few elements as needed. Self-supervised RL is discussed as a boundary case in structured interaction settings. Together, these recommendations place emphasis on deciding what RL is expected to adjust and how its value will be assessed.
icml-2026-position-rl-should-be-used-to-.tldr: RL should usually refine established foundation-model capabilities, with simple verifiable rewards and evaluation that accounts for compute costs.

paragraphs: This paper questions a measurement assumption underlying reinforcement learning from human feedback: that annotation responses express genuine preferences. Drawing on behavioral science, the authors explain that people may answer without an established opinion, construct a preference from contextual cues, or interpret identical questions differently. They argue that these problems are common in value judgments relevant to alignment.

The authors organize responses along a spectrum from non-attitudes, carrying no preference signal, to genuine preferences, carrying full signal. They develop diagnostics for locating responses on that spectrum. The key methodological claim is that researchers must establish what annotations measure before deciding how to aggregate them.

In two RLHF datasets, the paper finds systematic, directionally biased inconsistency. Removing highly inconsistent annotators reverses majority harm classifications for 18.6% of prompts and changes mean ratings by more than 13 points on a 100-point scale. These findings show that filtering can substantially alter the apparent collective judgment. They support the authors’ concern that current practice can treat elicitation artifacts and noise as evidence of human values.
icml-2026-position-rlhf-may-not-reflect-.tldr: Analysis of two RLHF datasets shows that inconsistent annotations can systematically distort the preferences and harm judgments attributed to people.

paragraphs: Single-cell perturbation analysis predicts how cellular states change after interventions. A central challenge is that measurements before and after an intervention usually describe unpaired populations. Learning the transition therefore also requires inferring which initial and later states correspond. This paper argues that the time between measurements is a key determinant of that problem’s difficulty.

Under biologically inspired conditions, the authors identify a critical time gap, Δ. Below it, recovering the matching is tractable in polynomial time and the remaining task becomes supervised learning. Above it, matching is NP-hard in the worst case. These results require restricted isometry of the initial states and temporal smoothness of the transition dynamics; the threshold claim is conditional on those assumptions.

Experiments on synthetic and biological datasets show a sharp change in regime as the measurement gap grows. The authors also demonstrate that a linear model can match or outperform higher-capacity neural approaches when their conditions hold. The findings connect experimental timing to both computational difficulty and effective model complexity, making measurement design directly relevant to the learning method needed.
icml-2026-position-temporal-measurement-.tldr: Under specified conditions, the measurement time gap separates tractable cell-state matching from worst-case hardness and affects the model complexity needed.

paragraphs: This position paper connects model collapse to concerns about who benefits from AI. Model collapse is performance degradation associated with training generative models on outputs from earlier models. The authors argue that growing amounts of generated content can make this phenomenon a threat to efforts to democratize AI.

Their argument brings together critiques of language models’ tendency to reproduce common patterns, dependence on large datasets, and environmental costs. Model collapse can shift data distributions away from less common content while reducing training efficiency. The paper argues that these effects disproportionately burden low-resource and marginalized communities, linking a technical degradation process to cultural exclusion and unequal access.

The authors examine environmental and cultural implications, place their position alongside recent discussions of collapse, and outline initial mitigation directions. Their central contribution is to frame data degradation as a distributional concern: the loss of less frequent patterns matters for communities already poorly represented in training material. Inefficient resource use adds another pressure to the same democratization goals.
icml-2026-position-the-stochastic-parrot.tldr: The paper argues that model collapse disproportionately threatens low-resource communities through loss of uncommon data patterns and reduced training efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper argues that current vision-language models lack an important form of visual agency: independently discovering and using evidence that has not been explicitly identified for them. The authors call this implicit reasoning. It requires a model to bridge information gaps through its own visual inquiry, beyond recognizing targets that a prompt already specifies.

The paper attributes this limitation to treating visual reasoning mainly as passive retrieval of semantic information. It argues that most existing benchmarks consequently measure passive capacity and leave autonomous exploration largely untested. To address that gap, the authors introduce the Visual Implicit Reasoning Diagnosing Benchmark, or V-IRD, which requires answers derived strictly through autonomous visual analysis.

The reported results show that prominent models struggle to use reference objects and attend to evidence requiring self-directed inquiry, despite strong retrieval abilities. This separates recognition performance from active evidence gathering. The contribution is both a diagnosis of that capability gap and a benchmark designed to expose it, making autonomous exploration a distinct target for evaluating visual reasoning.
icml-2026-position-the-systemic-lack-of-.tldr: V-IRD reveals that strong visual recognition can coexist with difficulty independently finding and using relevant visual evidence.

paragraphs: This position paper calls for research on token taxes as a response to AI automation’s economic risks. These taxes would add usage-based surcharges to model inference at the point of sale. The authors motivate the proposal through potential erosion of government revenues, lower living standards, and reduced citizen power.

The paper places token taxes within earlier proposals to tax robots and identifies two advantages: possible enforcement through existing compute-governance infrastructure and collection of value where AI is used rather than where models are hosted. It proposes a staged enforcement research agenda involving black-box token verification, norm-based rates, and white-box audits, with technical questions remaining at each stage.

The authors also call for economic modeling of how costs pass through to buyers and how taxation may reduce otherwise beneficial activity. They discuss whether taxes based on computation could be preferable, whether token taxes might inhibit innovation, and how powerful AI actors could obstruct adoption. The result is a research roadmap for evaluating feasibility and consequences, with the policy’s potential benefits weighed against explicit tradeoffs.
icml-2026-position-token-taxes-can-mitig.tldr: The paper proposes a technical and economic research agenda for usage-based AI taxes, including enforcement, cost pass-through, and innovation tradeoffs.

paragraphs: This position paper examines what happens when image generators are strongly aligned to a generalized idea of visual appeal. Artistic or critical intentions can call for deliberately unattractive, low-quality, or negative imagery. The authors argue that a system’s preference for conventional beauty can override those intentions and narrow the range of expression available to users.

To investigate, they construct a dataset spanning a broad range of aesthetics and evaluate leading generation and reward models. They find that aesthetically aligned generators frequently produce conventionally beautiful images despite instructions seeking contrary qualities. Reward models also penalize anti-aesthetic images even when those images fully satisfy the explicit prompt.

The authors further confirm this bias through image-to-image editing and evaluation involving real abstract artworks. The findings connect generation behavior with the evaluation signals used to judge images: both can favor generalized aesthetic preferences over requested expression. The paper argues that this pattern prioritizes developer-centered values and compromises user autonomy and aesthetic pluralism, particularly when the intended work deliberately challenges conventional beauty.
icml-2026-position-universal-aesthetic-a.tldr: Generation and reward models can favor conventional beauty even when users explicitly request anti-aesthetic imagery.

paragraphs: This position paper identifies two blind spots in benchmarks of causal reasoning for vision-language models. First, benchmarks may assume without testing that models understand time as the medium through which causes produce effects. Second, helpful prompt structure may supply reasoning support that substitutes for a capability the model has not internalized.

The authors draw on Cézanne’s painting technique to distinguish recording a single visual instant from constructing understanding through temporal integration. This serves as a conceptual lens for asking what visual intelligence requires. A fluent account of causation may still fail to represent a valid causal structure, so the form of the answer alone is insufficient to settle that question.

Preliminary evidence shows systematic differences between fluent causal text and valid causal structure, along with divergent responses to identical changes in scaffolding. The authors therefore call for benchmarks that test temporal understanding and robustness to scaffolding changes alongside output accuracy. The findings motivate closer examination of what prompt-assisted success reveals about the model’s underlying visual and causal capabilities.
icml-2026-position-what-cezanne-knew-abo.tldr: Preliminary evidence motivates visual-reasoning benchmarks that test temporal understanding and distinguish internal capability from prompt-provided scaffolding.
